name: Meadowgrass
lede: Meadowgrass is a dark, yellowish green from Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary, close enough to [[hunter-green|Hunter Green]] that the two likely come from the same part of the chart.

sections.title: A grass green, not a lawn green
sections.body:
Maerz and Paul place this value at plate 23, position H 9, first recorded in 1924 [1]. The ISCC-NBS system of 1955 classifies it as a dark yellowish green, about 3.2 units from that block's reference chip [2]. Unlike many of the dictionary's flower and animal names, meadowgrass needs no explanation: it is simply the grass of an open field, read as darker and more shadowed than a bright lawn [1].

Its nearest library neighbor is [[cossack|Cossack]], and it sits close to [[hunter-green|Hunter Green]], [[moss|Moss]] and [[olive-mud|Olive Mud]] on the same dark, muted stretch of the chart [2].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: In our archive of 23,781 paintings, a color within six units of Meadowgrass covers at least five per cent of the canvas in 119 works, about one in two hundred, as photographed [3]. Van Gogh, Pissarro and Gauguin each carry it at roughly sixteen times the rate expected for their output, and it peaks in paintings from the 1920s, over five times expected [3]. It functions mostly as a shadow color, and its company on canvas is mostly other greens, led by Hunter Green [3]. These remain photographs of aged, varnished canvases read as screen colors, not pigment tests [3].
